# Build and operate a DVM

Use `dvmctl` to manage the service and `@dvmkit/sdk` to implement its capabilities. Use the caller CLI, `dvm`, when testing the service as a customer. Keep its test wallet separate from the builder's keys and normal caller state.

## Choose the procedure

Identify the user's task and the service's current state. Read the matching file before acting. Load another only when the task crosses into its scope; an existing service does not need onboarding again.

| Task | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Turn an idea into a working local capability | [new-builder](new-builder.md) |
| Validate behavior or prove a paid call | [testing](testing.md), then only the chosen payment recipe |
| Build a job that prompts, charges mid-job, runs long, or has several capabilities | [work-shaped jobs](references/work-shaped-jobs.md) |
| Store the DVM's own data in Postgres | [builder tables](references/builder-tables.md) |
| Prepare or perform a deployment | [deploying](deploying.md) |
| Inspect health or earnings, collect payouts, refund a completed job, update, or transfer a service | [operating](operating.md) |
| Diagnose a failure or reconcile an uncertain payment or deploy | [recovery](recovery.md) |
| Retain job content for support or a dispute | [content holds](references/content-holds.md) |
| Export minimized financial evidence before database deletion | [financial export](references/financial-export.md) |
| Stop offering a service and close its outstanding obligations | [retirement](retirement.md) |

## Establish the context

Reuse the brief, decisions, and authorization already provided. Ask only for missing choices that affect the result, cost, access, or recoverability. An instruction to test locally does not authorize a production deployment or spending production funds.

Inspect the installed CLI version and the project's SDK dependency before selecting examples. Use the exact release and matching skill specified by the builder's setup. Do not upgrade an existing project merely to match an example. If versions disagree, establish the intended target before changing dependencies.

Before a remote change, confirm the service, organization, and environment from tool output. Names alone can identify the wrong service when an account belongs to several organizations.

## Rules that apply to every procedure

- Keep private keys, recovery words, payment credentials, and secret values out of chat, source, and logs. Use the documented secret-input mechanism. Never infer that a human has backed up recovery material.
- Keep the service's price separate from the authorized test-spend cap. Verify the network and payment destination before moving value. A development server can still accept real funds.
- When an outcome is uncertain, inspect the existing operation before retrying. A lost response does not prove that a payment or deployment failed. Continue through [recovery](recovery.md) when the tool cannot establish the result.
- Preserve recovery records until the relevant obligation is resolved. Unknown refund state is not a zero balance, and deleting a service does not settle its debts. Use [retirement](retirement.md) before destructive cleanup.
- Check user authorization before actions that spend funds, change payment destinations, transfer control, or destroy data. Existing authorization counts; do not ask for it again. Ask when the actual scope or consequence exceeds it.

The dvmkit team welcomes feedback at any time through `dvmctl feedback send`, especially about what was confusing, slow, or broken.

## Use the result

Read structured output and follow its recovery guidance. Relay `display` and `hint` when they answer the user's question. Check each command's contract: logs and exports need not be JSON.

Close a task with the observed result and the evidence relevant to it: a local artifact, a verified paid job, a live deployment, or a confirmed payout. When a local result closes a paid-service brief without deployment authorization, follow the deployment question in [new-builder](new-builder.md). Distinguish completed work from pending or unknown state. Never report a payout from a revenue total alone.

For exact syntax and output, read the [dvmctl reference](https://dvmkit.com/docs/cli-dvmctl.md). For handler interfaces, read the [SDK reference](https://dvmkit.com/docs/sdk.md). Use the [docs index](https://dvmkit.com/llms.txt) to retrieve other topics selectively.

# Public README

## Who the README is for

Two readers, in this order. First, a stranger's coding agent that has been told "use dvmkit" and lands on the GitHub page or the npm page with no other context. Second, a human skimming the same page to decide whether to try it. Neither is a maintainer, an operator of the hosted platform, or someone upgrading from last week's release; those readers have their own documents.

The test every README must pass: **an agent that reads only the README can install the package and finish its first useful action** (the first free job served, or the first DVM called, or the first DVM scaffolded). Everything in the README serves that test or the decision to try it. Material that serves neither goes somewhere else.

## Where a piece of content goes

Walk this for every paragraph, table and code block, including ones already in the README:

```
Does the reader need it to install, or to finish the first useful action?
├── Yes → README
└── No
    ├── Is it reference a builder or caller needs after the first run (options, rails, protocol, operations)?
    │   └── Yes → dvmkit.com docs; the README links the page in one line
    ├── Is it about what changed in a release, a migration, or an upgrade?
    │   └── Yes → CHANGELOG.md
    ├── Is it how this repository is built, tested, verified or released?
    │   └── Yes → docs/ in this repository (RELEASING.md, a maintainer doc), or AGENTS.md for agent working rules
    ├── Is it policy (contributions, security, support, conduct, trademarks)?
    │   └── Yes → its root file; the README carries at most two lines and a link
    └── Otherwise → delete it
```

Why: the README is the only page both readers are guaranteed to see, and every line of operator detail pushes the quickstart further from the top. One fact lives in one place; a copy in the README goes stale the first time the real home changes.

## Required shape, in this order

1. **Title and one sentence.** The package name, then what it is and who it is for, in plain words: a Digital Vending Machine is a pay-per-use HTTPS service an AI agent can find, pay and call with no account and no API key. Say what this package does within that (build one, call one, deploy one). No slogans.
2. **Status line.** One sentence: pre-1.0 alpha, breaking changes are announced in the [release notes](./CHANGELOG.md), pin the version you install. Use the word "alpha" and nothing else ("beta", "preview", "experimental" are banned), so the README, CHANGELOG, SECURITY.md and dvmkit.com agree.
3. **Requirements.** Runtime and minimum version, in one line.
4. **Install.** The command that resolves the current release: `npm install --save-exact @dvmkit/sdk`, `npm install --global @dvmkit/dvm-cli`. Never write a version number into an install command. Why: a pinned number in prose goes stale every release and silently sends readers to an old version; `--save-exact` still records the exact resolved version in the reader's own `package.json`.
5. **Quickstart.** The smallest sequence that reaches the first useful action, copy-pasteable top to bottom in an empty directory, with the expected output shown. It must be a verbatim copy of an example that this repository's CI runs (for the SDK, `examples/quickstart`); if the two differ, the README is wrong. At most 40 lines of code in total.
6. **For agents** (CLI repositories only). How an agent installs and loads the shipped skill (`dvm` or `build-dvm`), in at most five lines. The README points at the skill; it never copies the skill's content.
7. **What's in the package.** Entry points or commands as one short table: name and one-line purpose. Link the full reference instead of listing options.
8. **Next steps.** Three to six links to dvmkit.com docs pages, each with a few words on when to read it.
9. **Contributing, security, support.** One short paragraph each, linking CONTRIBUTING.md, SECURITY.md and SUPPORT.md.
10. **License.** One line naming the license with links to LICENSE and NOTICE, and one line linking TRADEMARKS.md if the repository has it. License is the last section.

Total length: at most 150 lines, and the quickstart's first command appears within the first 40 lines. Why: both readers decide in the first screen; a README longer than this is carrying content that belongs elsewhere.

## Never in a README

- Operator, hosting or platform-internal material: admin routes, `/_internal/` endpoints, hosting control, drain/closure, content holds, financial exports, retention schedules, diagnostic catalogues. Why: callers and builders cannot act on it, and it reads as the README of a different product.
- Wire-format grammar, header byte rules, fixture schemas. Link the protocol docs.
- Upgrade and migration notes, "older consumers must…", references to specific past versions. These are CHANGELOG content and are stale by the next release.
- Unsupported entry points, except one sentence saying they exist and carry no stability promise.
- Test-gate internals, timings, CI mechanics. Maintainer docs only.
- Literal email addresses. Link SUPPORT.md or SECURITY.md, which are the single place each address is written, so a change of address (or a switch to a form because of spam) is one edit.
- Private or internal names: tracker keys, internal hostnames, machine names, internal tool names, private repository names, private URLs.
- Claims you have not checked (see below), superlatives, and comparisons with named competitors.

## Code snippets

- Code snippets are TypeScript (`.ts`), because `dvmctl` scaffolds a TypeScript DVM and a builder should see the same language in the README as in the project they generate. Snippets run with Node's built-in type stripping (`node server.ts`, Node 22.18 or later), so the quickstart needs no build step and no extra dependency; state "Node.js 22.18 or later" in the quickstart's requirements line. Write only syntax Node can strip (no `enum`, no `namespace`, no parameter properties) and import local files with their `.ts` extension. Why: a snippet that needs a compiler the reader has not installed fails at the first command.
- Snippets run as shown in a fresh directory. If the package is ESM-only and the quickstart starts from `npm init -y`, add `npm pkg set type=module` as a step. Why: `npm init -y` creates a CommonJS project, and an ESM-only package imported there fails with an error a stranger's agent will misdiagnose.
- Show the expected output after any command that prints something the reader needs to check.
- Never put secrets, real keys, real wallet strings or real endpoints in a snippet; use `example.com` and obviously fake values.

## Checking before you commit

1. Run every command and snippet in the README in a fresh temporary directory, against the published package or, for an unreleased change, a tarball packed from this repository (`npm pack`). A snippet you did not run does not go in.
2. Request every link and confirm it answers 200 at its final URL. Docs and site links use `dvmkit.com`, never `dvmkit.ai` (that domain hosts DVM endpoints, and its site paths only redirect).
3. Compare the install command, status word, runtime requirement and quickstart with the matching dvmkit.com docs page. If they disagree, say so in your hand-off; the site is fixed in its own repository, never by copying site text into the README.
4. Walk the "Where a piece of content goes" tree over the whole diff, then check the length budget.
5. Fresh-agent test for a rewrite: a new session with only the README must reach the first useful action. What trips it up is the edit list.

## This repository

- Package: `@dvmkit/dvmctl`. First useful action: install the CLI and the `build-dvm` skill, then scaffold a DVM and prove a local job works.
- The README has no code quickstart; its commands (installs, skill copy, `dvmctl create`) are verified in a fresh temporary HOME against `npm pack` output.
- Matching site pages: https://dvmkit.com/docs/build-quickstart and https://dvmkit.com/docs/cli-dvmctl.

# Test value

Apply repository verification and ownership rules first. Tests protect behavior or an independent contract; counts and coverage percentages do not establish that protection.

## Before writing a test

Identify the behavior, a plausible defect, and why existing tests miss it. Choose the cheapest boundary that exposes that defect. A second layer needs a distinct failure to catch. Mock external inputs, not the behavior being asserted. Prefer extending existing cases when they own the same contract.

Expected results must come from a specification, independently derived example, or meaningful property. Fixture self-checks, configured mock output, self-comparisons, and expected values computed by the same implementation do not qualify. Determinism, round trips, idempotence and retry/replay are valid when a production defect can violate the property.

For a bug fix, demonstrate that the test fails for the intended reason without the fix, then passes with it. If that control cannot run, state the missing evidence. Avoid production exports, switches, or indirection used only to reach implementation details; first seek an existing observable boundary.

## Audit an existing suite

1. **Set the boundary.** Pin the baseline revision. Inventory owned test files, support code, generated tests and CI routing. Name which files receive a full semantic review and which receive only candidate searches. Record baseline test results and existing failures separately. Use available coverage tooling as supporting evidence; do not install a coverage or mutation framework merely for cleanup.
2. **Read before judging.** Read candidate tests including tables, their production owner, callers and relevant history. Identify what each assertion actually detects. Look for vacuous negatives, fixtures doing the work, assertions weaker than their names, repeated proof at multiple layers, and source-spelling checks. These are candidates, not automatic deletions.
3. **Record decisions.** For each declaration in the fully reviewed group, mark retain, repair, consolidate or delete, with a short reason. For each proposed removal/repair, record location, credible defect, remaining proof or absence of a meaningful contract, history, affected support code and focused validation. Group repetitive retained cases only when they share the same reasoning; account for distinct table rows.
4. **Compare layers.** Name the retained suite for each contract before editing. Move unique assertions into it before retiring duplicates. Remove support or production access points only after checking all callers and supported API obligations. Similar syntax or a slower test does not prove redundancy.
5. **Apply a coherent batch.** Preserve separate money, recovery, lifecycle, package/release, security and architecture protection. Source inspection can be appropriate when the source property is itself the contract; check a deliberately invalid example. Treat failing baseline tests as possible product defects, never cleanup opportunities. Keep substantial unrelated fixes separate.
6. **Verify preservation.** Run affected retained tests and required repository gates after edits. Use a deliberate defect or invalid input to show changed protection fails for the intended reason; restore any temporary source change exactly before continuing. Do not edit a checkout during its test run. Have an independent reviewer compare removed assertions with retained proof and resolve gaps before landing.

Keep a compact audit record with scope, decisions, evidence, baseline/final test and support size, separately counted production changes, actual checks and skips. Rerun discovery when upstream changes the audited owner. No deletion target, weaker gate, increased timeout, or acceptable coverage drop authorizes losing a distinct contract. A justified retention is a completed audit decision.

## Comments and scope

Do not add tests solely for prose or policy wording. Preserve useful rationale, API semantics, functional annotations and tooling directives while removing comment noise. Tests do not justify otherwise dead production paths. Follow normal review, delivery and CI ownership rules; this skill grants no publication or permission changes.

Method informed by [OpenClaw's test-audit skill](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/.agents/skills/test-audit/SKILL.md), adapted to local verification and test-ownership rules.

# dvmctl

Build and deploy Digital Vending Machines: pay-per-use HTTPS services that AI agents can find, pay, and call with no account or API key. Ships the `build-dvm` agent skill.

Alpha software. This is a pre-1.0 alpha; breaking changes are announced in the [release notes](./CHANGELOG.md).

## Install

Node.js 22 or later and npm are required.

Install the CLI:

```bash
npm install --global @dvmkit/dvmctl
```

## For agents

Install the complete bundled skill directory so its task modules and payment recipes remain available. For Claude Code:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root --global)/@dvmkit/dvmctl/skills/build-dvm" ~/.claude/skills/
```

## Upgrade details

- Add `dvmctl refund <job-id>` for full or partial completed-job refunds onto the caller's credit. Confirmation is required before any HTTP request. Stable refund IDs make retries return the original result; `--refund-id` permits a deliberate additional partial refund.
- Pin the CLI runtime and new project scaffolds to exact `@dvmkit/sdk` `0.37.0`. Separately installed project dependencies stay unchanged until explicitly upgraded. `dvmctl serve` and `dvmctl dev` run the CLI's pinned SDK, so upgrading or downgrading dvmctl changes their SDK on the next restart. A project's own `serve.ts` uses its installed SDK. Pause monetary writes and coordinate upgrades or rollbacks across these processes under the rules below, even when the project's own SDK dependency is unchanged. Custom credit stores must implement the SDK's transactional `refundDraw` accounting and report enqueueing.
- With PostgreSQL and `DVMKIT_DVM_ID`, settlement history and reporting identity now initialize at boot without hosting-control settings. Fresh databases start with complete history; existing incomplete or missing historical evidence is not certified by upgrading. Reporting identity inherits the single scope owning the DVM's obligations, and ambiguous historical scope or instance ownership refuses boot. The SDK removes hosting-control exports, options and routes; its former environment variables are ignored. The CLI and starter do not use those APIs.
- Authenticated object input schemas must declare `pubkey`, `signature`, `timestamp` and `nonce`, or preserve unknown fields. Capabilities remain on the job channel by default; adding x402 channels requires explicit job-channel selection, bounded runtime and pricing. Upgrade every instance sharing a job database before serving x402 channel jobs, since older instances do not preserve the channel during recovery. The starter remains an unauthenticated job-channel capability.
- Before activating refunds, pause monetary writes and upgrade every process sharing the credit database and report queue, including funding writers and retry workers. Mixed-version monetary history after new metadata is written needs a state compatibility assessment, as does rollback after refund state exists. Older readers cannot interpret refund reports or known-zero Bitcoin lots. Additive schema initialization alone does not make a rolling upgrade or rollback safe. If enabling hosted Stripe Checkout, upgrade all processes sharing its store together and keep Checkout-aware recovery running until recorded sessions resolve before rollback. See [refund guidance](docs/refund-command.md) and the [SDK upgrade details](https://github.com/dvmkit/sdk/blob/v0.37.0/CHANGELOG.md).

# Releasing dvmctl

## Scope

Only the standalone dvmctl repository publishes `@dvmkit/dvmctl`. Stable releases publish to `latest`, and RC releases publish to `next`. Both require publicly verifiable provenance.

## Operator configuration evidence

Before enabling publication, record that npm trusted publishing is bound to the `dvmkit/dvmctl` repository, `release.yml` workflow, `npm-release` environment, and direct `npm publish` permission. The npm connection must be permitted to publish directly rather than stage-only. No npm token is used.

Record that the GitHub environment accepts stable `vX.Y.Z` and RC `vX.Y.Z-rc.N` tags. Record that the release App is repository-only, has only contents, issues, and pull-request write permissions, and cannot bypass rulesets. Record that only maintainers can create stable and RC tags and that no actor can update or delete them.

## Compatibility

The exact SDK selection is `dependencies["@dvmkit/sdk"]` in [package.json](package.json); `node scripts/sdk-version.mjs` prints it. Artifact checks, consumer installs, and scaffolds read it. Update it and the lockfile only after the selected registry version exists. It supports Node.js `>=22` and is built with Node.js `22.23.2`.

## Full package acceptance without publishing

Use [consumer-smoke.mjs](scripts/consumer-smoke.mjs) to check an installed archive from an immutable reviewed source revision. This needs only public source and npm packages, Node.js **22.23.2**, npm **10.9.8**, Git, Bash, `tar`, and a running Docker engine. Allow outbound npm/image downloads, local listeners, and enough writable temporary space for several npm installs and Docker builds. Use a disposable host or Docker daemon with no platform credentials, publication credentials, or wallet funds.

| Mode | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Default (omit `--full`) | Scaffold install, generated tests/typecheck, validation, dev with reload and `--no-reload`, serving SDK banner/development page, matching and mismatched project SDKs, completed free local jobs with retained artifacts, and refusal to serve without a production database. |
| `--full` | All default checks plus production serving and completed local jobs with PostgreSQL, serving SDK/mismatch checks in production, Docker build-context exclusions, runtime SDK/`pg` dependencies and development-dependency pruning, and deployment request/archive contracts against local fixtures. |

The [Verify workflow](.github/workflows/verify.yml) packs twice and runs default mode against that installed archive across its runtime matrix. The [Release workflow](.github/workflows/release.yml) runs full mode before publication and against the exact published version afterward. Deployment responses in this fixture are simulated: full mode does not deploy a live platform service, exercise machine control/database tunnels, or prove paid calls or refunds. Those need separate platform/payment acceptance.

### Run the procedure

Run this block in Bash. Replace `REVIEWED_COMMIT` with the independently reviewed full 40-character source commit, never a branch or npm dist-tag. By default it builds a candidate twice from that revision using the existing [release artifact identity checks](scripts/release-artifact.mjs); retain the resulting archive and digest as the candidate under review. `v$version` and the channel here are identity fields only; no tag is created and nothing is published.

For an **already reviewed archive**, download and extract the artifact from the specific matching Verify or Release run, recording its run URL and checked-out source SHA (a PR run can use a merge commit). Set `reviewed_artifact_dir` below to that directory's absolute path. It must contain the original `release-digest.json` and exactly one `.tgz`. Do not regenerate a digest for an unverified download. Both paths verify against the independently expected source commit/version/channel before installation; no npm dist-tag selects the CLI or SDK.

### Cleanup and evidence checklist

The fixture attempts to stop serving process groups and close fixture HTTP servers, then removes its `dvmctl-consumer-*` temporary directory (including scaffolds, config, and job artifacts). A failed process stop can leave that directory for diagnosis. The runtime Docker container uses `--rm`, and the fixture attempts to remove its `dvmctl-consumer-*` runtime image. Image-removal failures are tolerated, and cleanup errors can be hidden by a primary test failure. The deploy dry run leaves an untagged image; downloaded base images and Docker build cache also remain.

After **every attempt**, inspect `result.txt`, `cleanup.log` if present, and the before/after runtime-image inventories. Confirm the named PostgreSQL container and its anonymous volume are gone and no fixture processes/containers remain. A failed attempt retains the scratch directory recorded in `scratch-directory.txt`; save diagnostics, stop any remaining processes, then remove that directory. If interrupted before the exit trap completes, explicitly run `docker rm --force --volumes <recorded-container-name>` using `postgres-name.txt` and perform the same scratch cleanup. Remove leftover runtime images by their exact recorded tag. Use a disposable Docker daemon to discard untagged images, base images, and build cache without pruning unrelated work. Delete the retained evidence directory only after saving the review record.

Record in the pull request:

- Full source commit, artifact origin/run URL when downloaded, CLI version, archive filename and SHA-256 from `release-digest.json`; retain that digest and the exact archive.
- Archive SDK pin and installed SDK version from `installed-versions.json`, plus Node/npm versions and host OS/Docker version.
- The full-mode command with its installed CLI path represented by a public-safe placeholder, result/exit status, and relevant assertion failure if any.
- Cleanup outcome separately: process/scratch removal, database/container/volume removal, runtime image leftovers, and intentionally retained evidence or Docker cache. A passing job alone does not prove cleanup.

Keep raw logs locally for reproduction. Before publishing evidence, remove local filesystem paths, host/account identifiers, credentials, and unrelated environment data. This procedure does not replace the repository's `npm run verify` gate or the hosted package/runtime checks.

## Prepare a stable release or release candidate

Release-please creates a version and changelog pull request when the repository variable `RELEASE_PLEASE_ENABLED` is `true`. Package, lockfile, and release manifest must agree. For fresh history, use release-please manifest bootstrap and first-release controls. The package and release manifest start at `0.5.0-rc.5`, so the first fresh-history release needs a `Release-As: 0.8.0` commit footer to select the intended stable version. Ordinary merges never publish.

After that pull request is merged, use the stable tag form for a stable release:

```sh
node scripts/release-tag.mjs --tag vX.Y.Z --dry-run
node scripts/release-tag.mjs --tag vX.Y.Z
git push origin vX.Y.Z
```

For a release candidate, use the RC tag form:

```sh
node scripts/release-tag.mjs --tag vX.Y.Z-rc.N --dry-run
node scripts/release-tag.mjs --tag vX.Y.Z-rc.N
git push origin vX.Y.Z-rc.N
```

The helper requires a clean live default-branch tip, an absent tag, and a separate SSH signing probe. The release workflow accepts only an annotated, allowed-signer stable or RC tag. It resolves the tagged commit and its unique merged release PR once, builds the package twice, and publishes only the resulting same-run artifact to the version's dist-tag with `--provenance`.

## Recover a disrupted release

Never retag, unpublish, overwrite, or move a dist-tag to recover a release. The publisher accepts an existing version only when its tarball digest and channel dist-tag exactly match the reviewed artifact. Recovery also requires cryptographically verified npm provenance bound to the exact archive, repository, release workflow, signed tag, and prepared commit. Missing attestations wait within the same bound; invalid signatures or source bindings fail.

npm malware scanning can hold an accepted upload for more than 15 minutes after `npm publish` exits successfully. Registry visibility and the subsequent exact-version consumer install each receive a separate 30-minute retry budget, polling every 15 seconds. Requests and install attempts add to that elapsed time; these are retry budgets rather than strict wall-clock deadlines. The release jobs use GitHub's default 360-minute job timeout, which exceeds the retry budgets and leaves time for setup.

If visibility times out, npm may still be processing the accepted upload. Keep the existing signed tag and reviewed archive, and wait for that exact npm version to become visible. Then manually dispatch the Release workflow with the existing tag and `github_release_recovery=true` to restore GitHub release notes and the release-PR labels:

```sh
gh workflow run release.yml --ref master -f tag=vX.Y.Z -f github_release_recovery=true
```

Use `vX.Y.Z-rc.N` for a release candidate. Recovery verifies and builds the tagged commit, then checks the exact registry bytes, dist-tag, and provenance before changing notes or labels. Omit `github_release_recovery` to verify and build the tag only. Manual dispatch never publishes; do not start another upload just because the visibility wait timed out.

## Migrations and rollback

Document user-visible command or scaffold migrations in the release pull request and changelog. To roll back, publish a later stable release for `latest`, or a later RC for `next`, that restores the required behavior; do not replace an immutable artifact. Stable tags use `vX.Y.Z`; RC tags use `vX.Y.Z-rc.N`. Stable publication requires `latest` to match the version; RC publication preserves the stable `latest` observed beforehand. Public provenance requires a public source repository at publication time. Recreating the repository requires rebinding the npm trusted-publisher identity to its new repository ID.

# Hosting billing and trial recovery

`dvmctl billing status` reads the platform's billing-state version 1 without buying a plan, creating an account, starting a trial, or changing a restriction. Output is JSON by default; add `--human` for prose on stderr, including relevant amounts, deadlines, next steps, and the request trace ID. The JSON response retains canonical money units, service periods, reservations, cost breakdowns, coverage, deadlines, restriction codes, and all allowed next actions. Unknown coverage is not zero usage. Read every restriction: paying one balance does not remove other holds.

| Command | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `billing status` | Inspect billing, trial admission, allowances, and recovery. |
| `billing budget get` | Read the budget and its concurrency version. |
| `billing budget set <usd-cents\|none> --expected-version <n> --idempotency-key <key>` | Explicitly set or remove a budget. The platform enforces authorisation and plan eligibility. |
| `billing topup <usd-cents> --idempotency-key <key>` | Explicitly request a Lightning hosting invoice; minimum 1000 USD cents. |
| `billing topup-status <id>` | Poll an existing hosting top-up once. |
| `billing plan quote <plan-id> --request-key <key>` | Obtain a plan-change quote without purchasing. Requires an existing settled paid term. |
| `billing plan purchase <quote-id> --rail stripe\|lightning` | Explicitly purchase a saved quote. |
| `billing plan status <quote-id>` | Inspect or reconcile an already requested plan change. |
| `billing checkout <plan-id> --rail stripe\|lightning [--months 1\|3\|6\|12]` | Explicitly request checkout, including a trial-to-paid conversion. Months apply only to Lightning. |
| `billing invoice <invoice-id>` | Poll an existing Lightning subscription invoice once. |
| `trial export <slug> [--port <port>] [--machine <id>]` | Open the existing read-only database tunnel during the seven-day recovery window. |
| `trial restore <slug>` | Request restore after verified purchase, including after the seven-day recovery deadline if a paid plan was purchased before it; never purchase or reset the trial. |

All commands accept `--human` and `--org <handle>`. Organisation selection, including the context saved by `dvmctl switch`, applies to status, budgets, top-ups, Stripe checkout, and trial recovery. The platform's plan-change and Lightning subscription routes bill only the authenticated key's account. Those commands reject a selected organisation rather than charging another account. Use a key for the intended account and `dvmctl switch --personal` for those routes. Organisation keys cannot edit budgets; the platform requires an authorised builder key.

Save the idempotency key before a top-up or budget write and reuse the exact arguments after an interruption. Keys contain 8–128 letters, digits, underscores, or hyphens. A budget update also requires the version observed by `budget get`; a conflict requires reading the budget before deciding on a new mutation. Save the request key when creating a quote, and reuse that key and target to retrieve the same quote. Purchase retries use the saved quote id. Renewal-downgrade quotes require the platform's scheduling workflow; this CLI does not schedule them.

A hosted Stripe URL or Lightning invoice is a human payment step. It is never proof of payment. Output includes the invoice id or URL and a `continuation.status_command` argument array. Hosting top-up output retains both the USD hosting value and the native invoice amount, plus invoice expiry timestamps in Unix milliseconds. Subscription Lightning checkout and invoice output retains `fiatCurrency` and `planUsdCents` when supplied. `amount_display` labels `amountCents` in that reporting currency; `plan_usd_display` shows the canonical USD plan value before subscription credit and excluding compute overage, or null when unknown. Invalid currency codes are shown beside the raw minor-unit amount, preserving the invoice id for continuation. On older platforms without these fields, the invoice currency is explicitly unstated and never assumed to be USD. Plan-change purchases use the saved quote currency. Quote output uses the quote's currency. A top-up's `quote.expiresAt` and `providerExpiresAt` are separate authorities and both remain visible. Only the platform's `paid` top-up status confirms credit; subscription statuses such as `payment_received` and `payment_recovery` still need reconciliation.

Resume an interrupted Lightning flow with `billing invoice <invoice-id>` or `billing topup-status <id>`, not another checkout. Stripe and Lightning subscription checkout do not accept idempotency keys on this platform; dvmctl does not retry those POST requests automatically. Inspect billing and any saved invoice before explicitly requesting another checkout.

For an expired trial, inspect `billing status`, then run `trial export <slug>` while recovery remains available. Keep the command running, and supply its `database_url` to `pg_dump` to write an export file. That URL contains temporary credentials; keep it private. The platform makes the recovery login read-only and ends the socket by the original recovery deadline. An export failure or retry does not extend that deadline. Use explicit `billing checkout` to buy a paid plan, confirm payment, then run `trial restore <slug>`. Other holds can still prevent restore; `trial_restore_blocked` relays the platform display. The restore response does not carry restriction reasons. When the follow-up billing-state read succeeds, dvmctl copies its restriction rows into `reasons`; those rows can include holds on other DVMs in the account. If the read fails, the reasons are unavailable. A `trial_recovery_closed` response means the recovery window ended; it does not assert that the DVM was destroyed.

Deploy, scale, and resume refusals preserve `reasons`, `display`, `hint`, and `options`. For hosting admission codes or refusals carrying restriction reasons, if no next actions are supplied, dvmctl follows the refusal with a billing-state read for the same account. The refusal keeps its own trace id, with the billing read identified separately as `billing_state_trace_id`. The original refusal remains authoritative if that follow-up fails, with `billing_state_error` and a status-command continuation.

An unknown billing-state version produces `billing_version_unsupported` and asks for a dvmctl upgrade before interpreting the response. Unknown reason and action codes in version 1 pass through. A missing gated route on an older platform produces `billing_not_available`: the feature is not available on that platform. A JSON `not_found` response means the invoice, quote, or top-up identifier is absent or inaccessible. A plain-text 404 on those gated status routes means the feature is unavailable on that platform.

# Refund a completed job

`dvmctl refund <job-id>` restores all or part of a completed job's charge to the caller's original prepaid credit. The caller can spend it on another job or reclaim it with `dvm credit drain <dvm>`. Per-job payments, Tempo channel credits, and x402 batch-channel credits are unsupported.

Run it in the service's project directory, or select the service with `--dvm <slug>`. The default name comes from the project, as for `deploy`. `--org <handle>` selects the organization, including the context saved by `dvmctl switch`. `--endpoint <url>` uses the existing signed admin connection for a self-hosted or local service.

```sh
dvmctl refund job-example --dvm scrape
dvmctl refund job-example --dvm scrape --confirm
dvmctl refund job-another --dvm scrape --amount 0.003 --reason "Incomplete result" --confirm
```

Without `--confirm`, the command refuses with `confirmation_required` and describes a local intent. It sends no HTTP, including discovery or admin requests. The intent does not establish eligibility or a numeric remainder. An explicit amount is a decimal in the job's credit currency; this local intent does not guess that currency. Omit `--amount` to refund the remaining unrefunded charge. Explicit amounts must be positive, have at most six fractional digits, and fit a safe integer number of micro-units. Exponents and rounding are unsupported. Reasons are optional and at most 280 characters.

The default refund ID depends on the immutable DVM ID, job ID, and normalized amount intent. `0.003` and `00.003000` identify the same refund. A remainder intent stays the same after other balance activity. Repeat the original arguments after an interruption: the server returns the original refund without changing the balance again. Preserve the reason, too; changing it while reusing the ID causes `refund_conflict`.

To deliberately issue another partial refund of the same amount for the same job, choose and retain a new ID:

```sh
dvmctl refund job-another --dvm scrape --amount 0.003 --refund-id support-refund-second --confirm
```

JSON is the default. `display` and `hint` explain what the caller sees; `--human` relays the same semantics. Success retains `status`, `refund_id`, `credit_id`, `draw_id`, `job_id`, `amount_micro`, `currency`, `ledger_seq`, `refunded_at`, `balance_after_micro`, and `replayed`. On replay, the monetary values, timestamp, sequence, and balance snapshot describe the original refund. `balance_after_micro` is not a current balance after later activity.

The service checks eligibility and cumulative refunds atomically. Closed credits and channel-backed payments cannot be forced through this command. `credit_refund_basis_unavailable` requires an operator to inspect independent original-payment evidence; current exchange rates cannot replace it. `credit_refund_state_unavailable` requires independent funding and drain evidence. Retrying alone repairs neither. `credit_refund_unavailable` means the persistent credit store or platform refund reporter needs configuration; no refund was queued. Repair configuration, then repeat the original ID and arguments.

## Upgrade before activation

The CLI and new scaffolds use exact `@dvmkit/sdk` `0.11.0-rc.1`. Separately installed project dependencies stay unchanged until explicitly upgraded. `dvmctl serve` and `dvmctl dev` run the CLI's pinned SDK, so upgrading or downgrading dvmctl changes their SDK on the next restart. Pause monetary writes and coordinate upgrades or rollbacks across these processes under the rules below, even when the project's own SDK dependency is unchanged. The development memory ledger cannot serve this refund route; production refunds require persistent credit storage and a transactional platform refund reporter.

Before enabling refunds, pause monetary writes and upgrade every process sharing the credit database and report queue, including funding writers and retry workers. Older writers can invalidate funding-order evidence, and older readers cannot interpret refund reports or known-zero Bitcoin lots. Mixed-version monetary history after the new metadata starts being written requires a state compatibility assessment. Assess rollback compatibility after refund state exists. Additive schema initialization alone does not make a rolling upgrade or rollback safe. See the [SDK upgrade details](https://github.com/dvmkit/sdk/blob/v0.11.0-rc.1/CHANGELOG.md).

# Deploy or update a DVM

Use this for first deployment and later revisions. Reuse existing authorization; ask only when the target, costs, funds, or destructive effects exceed it.

## Establish the target

Inspect the project's SDK version, handler, build inputs, and deployment configuration. Read the [hosting explanation](https://dvmkit.com/docs/deploying.md) and the [deploy command contract](https://dvmkit.com/docs/cli-dvmctl.md#deploy) for the chosen target.

For Cloud, run `dvmctl auth --status`, `dvmctl orgs`, and `dvmctl whoami`. Select the intended organization with `dvmctl switch` only when needed. If login is missing (`auth_required`), a human must sign in once, and the human may be on another machine. Either run `dvmctl auth` and relay the printed link and session code to them (they can open it on any device within 5 minutes, and signing in also creates the account if they have none), keeping the command running until it reports authenticated; or, if you cannot wait or run unattended, ask them to create an API key in the dashboard and set `DVMKIT_API_KEY`. See [authentication](https://dvmkit.com/docs/cli-auth.md). Never create or switch an account merely to get past an access refusal.

Use `dvmctl auth --no-browser` to relay the link without launching a local browser, or set `BROWSER` to an isolated browser command or profile (quoted arguments are supported; `%s` is replaced by the URL, otherwise the URL is appended; no shell expansion). The single JSON `awaiting_human` event reports whether launch succeeded; always relay the link and session code. `dvmctl auth --logout` attempts server-side revocation of the stored key and clears local credentials; if `revoked` is false, follow its manual revocation hint.

For an update, record the existing deployment and inspect outstanding jobs and payment obligations. Preserve their database and keys across the update. Establish the effective resources and costs from the current plan; do not promise an unverified spending cap.

## Prepare keys and payment operations

Builder signing keys, Cashu recovery words, and records live in `~/.dvmkit` (`builder.key`, `builder.mnemonic`, and `builder.json`). Set `DVMKIT_CONFIG_DIR` before inspecting or creating them to select a separate builder tree. Authentication uses `~/.dvmctl` and `DVMCTL_CONFIG_DIR`; caller wallet state uses `~/.dvm` and `DVM_CONFIG_DIR`. Changing the authentication directory does not move builder secrets.

An explicit `DVMKIT_CONFIG_DIR` disables automatic legacy mnemonic migration. If `lock create` or `deploy` names an untouched legacy file, have the human use `dvmctl lock create --import <words>` in a private terminal to reuse those words. To create independent words instead, use `dvmctl lock create --force --human`; the legacy file stays in place. Keep recovery words out of agent output.

A real deployment needs a builder signing identity. Inspect it with `dvmctl identity show`; create one only if absent and authorized. `dvmctl deploy --create-identity` can create the missing identity noninteractively. The account is bound to one signing key: on another machine, if creation fails with `identity_bound_elsewhere`, have the human run `dvmctl identity import` (secret on stdin or `--from-file`, never an argument) in a private terminal. `dvmctl whoami` reports whether the local identity matches. Never replace an existing identity to bypass an error.

If accepting Cashu, establish the lock identity and recovery backup. When creation is needed, have the human run `dvmctl lock create --human` in a private terminal and save the recovery words. Do not capture the words in agent output. Require explicit confirmation that the backup is complete before accepting production funds.

Read [payments and payouts](https://dvmkit.com/docs/builder-payments.md) and the SDK's [payment environment](https://dvmkit.com/docs/sdk.md#payment-rail-environment-variables) only for the chosen methods. Verify the production network or mints, recipient, and required worker:

- Cashu needs the recovery keys, payout destination, and refund/payout worker.
- Lightning credit needs durable credit storage and a receive-only `DVMKIT_NWC_RECEIVE_URI`. Prepare the separate refund worker; the DVM's receiving connection must not spend.
- Stablecoin channels need settlement and close handling. Self-hosted Tempo sessions need the documented close observer.
- One-payment stablecoin credit needs the explicit opt-in and manual refund process before it is offered.

## Preview and submit

A Cloud deployment packages only files git can see, so the project must be a committed git repository with a `Dockerfile` at its root (or at the named build context) before `deploy` will proceed: it refuses a missing Dockerfile and an uncommitted packaged tree. Commit the intended source first, and keep untracked helper files out of the build.

Run project checks, `dvmctl validate`, and `dvmctl doctor`. Preview with `dvmctl deploy --dry-run`; a container preview requires Docker. Resolve failures before a real submission. Do not bypass a dirty-source refusal without an explicit reason and authorization for the exact source being deployed.

A Cloud deployment uploads the DVM folder and nothing above it. When the Dockerfile needs a containing folder, such as a workspace root that holds the lockfile, name that folder in `package.json` as `dvmkit.buildContext` (relative to the DVM folder, for example `"../.."`) or pass `--context`; the folder must contain the DVM folder and stay inside the repository. A DVM without its own lockfile under a repository folder that has one is refused until the context is named. Credential stores such as `.ssh` and `.dvmkit` are never uploaded. Both deploy and dry-run JSON report the uploaded folder as `context_root` and the Dockerfile as `dockerfile`.

For Cloud, supply secret values through a secret manager into `dvmctl deploy --env-stdin` as the documented JSON string map. This option is Cloud-only and is not accepted by dry-run. Do not put secrets in command arguments, source, or logs. This is also why a secret the service needs at first start belongs in `--env-stdin` on that deploy: `dvmctl env <slug> --set KEY=value` after deploy passes the value as an argument, visible in shell history and process listings. Use `dvmctl env` for non-secret settings, and change a secret by redeploying with `--env-stdin` under the same authorization as any deploy. Stdin values override the project `.env`. Inspect `.env` as an input boundary without printing its values: Cloud deployment reads it too.

Submit the authorized deployment once and retain its deployment ID. For an ambiguous response, inspect `dvmctl deploy-status <id>` and the service before retrying; use [recovery](recovery.md) when the result remains unknown.

For self-hosting, initialize the durable service ID with `dvmctl init <slug> --self-hosted`, then run `dvmctl deploy --target self-host`. Protect any generated attestation and receipt-key values as secrets. Deploy the generated container with the target's tools, configure its durable database and secrets, and operate the required payment workers yourself. Generating these files is not a completed deployment.

## Control discovery

For an unlisted launch, deploy first, then run `dvmctl visibility <slug> --hidden`. The DVM can appear in discovery between deployment and the visibility change; deployment cannot create it hidden. Hiding only removes it from discovery: anyone with its URL can still call it, so visibility is not access control.

Run `dvmctl visibility <slug> --listed` to restore discovery. Choose exactly one of `--hidden` or `--listed`. Both require an admin role in the DVM's organization. Use `--org <handle>` to override the active organization selected by `dvmctl switch`, and `--human` for terminal output. Default JSON returns `{ slug, hidden }`. Check the current state with `dvmctl info <slug>` or `dvmctl list`; both also show visibility with `--human`.

## Verify the deployed service

Inspect the actual endpoint, active revision, and health. Read `/v1/info` or `dvm describe` to confirm capability, price, any declared rate card, signing identity, and intended payment configuration. Test the agreed example and retrieve its output.

A Cloud deploy of a DVM with x402 routes also asks Coinbase's public x402 validator about each route and reports the verdict under `x402_listing`: `listed`, `listed_with_problems` (each failed check, with a fix where one is known), `not_listed` (no catalog listing, which is optional), `unreachable`, `not_x402`, `challenge_invalid` (the route answers 402 but its payment challenge fails Coinbase's checks), or `check_unavailable`. The check never changes the deploy's status. Run `dvmctl x402 listing-check <slug>` to repeat it, for example after a `deployed_unverified` deploy.

For a production paid acceptance, follow [testing](testing.md) with the already approved funds and cap. If that scope is absent, report the deployment evidence and the specific paid check still unperformed. Never claim receipt or payout from a successful build alone.

Record the endpoint, deployed revision, validation result, and any pending payment operation. Continue to [operating](operating.md) for earnings and payout work.

Reuse the supplied brief. Ask only for missing decisions that affect the result: capability name, typed input, expected output, one input-to-result example, and price. Establish external provider costs if the handler will call a paid API. Keep the paid-test cap separate from the service price.

Start with one capability unless the brief needs more. Record the agreed example in the project so validation and the final report use the same expectation. Defer production payment and hosting choices until they are needed by the authorized task.

## Implement the handler

For a new scaffold:

```bash
dvmctl create my-dvm
cd my-dvm
npm install
```

Use the scaffold's pinned SDK. For a handwritten project, pin the SDK version admitted by the installed CLI and skill. Read only the relevant parts of the [SDK reference](https://dvmkit.com/docs/sdk.md): [descriptor](https://dvmkit.com/docs/sdk.md#configuredvm), [input](https://dvmkit.com/docs/sdk.md#input-validation-with-zod), and [job context](https://dvmkit.com/docs/sdk.md#the-job-context).

Implement the agreed input and result. Validate input with the SDK's exported Zod instance. Use the SDK's completion and artifact APIs so callers can retrieve and verify the result. For dynamic pricing, storage, or external side effects, load the corresponding SDK section before selecting an interface. When the price is quoted or tiered, declare a [rate card](https://dvmkit.com/docs/sdk.md#rate-cards) so the storefront and callers' agents see the per-unit rates before quoting.

Mock the external dependency for handler tests, then use a separately authorized live check to prove the provider accepts the actual request shape. A mocked response does not establish that contract.

## Prove the local result

Run the project's tests and typecheck, then:

```bash
dvmctl validate
dvmctl doctor
dvmctl dev handler.ts
```

Read the dev banner before calling it. Payment verification is skipped only when no rail is configured; a configured rail can move real value. Use the printed `/_dev` interface or caller command to run the agreed example. Use `/_dev` when the caller CLI is not installed; the paid-test recipes install their own isolated caller. For an object input, the HTTP request uses `data`; the caller CLI uses `--data`.

Retrieve the terminal result and any advertised artifacts. Compare their contents with the agreed example, not only the command's exit status. If the handler fails, fix it before adding payment complexity.

Report the implemented capability, observed result, and artifact location. Continue to [testing](testing.md) for paid evidence or to [deploying](deploying.md) when those tasks are already authorized.

When deployment is not authorized and the brief describes callers paying (a price, a payment rail, or charging callers), end the report by asking once whether to deploy. Skip the question when the brief says the service is local-only or test-only, and never ask it twice in a task. Say in plain words what deploying involves: the human signs in to dvmkit in a browser, hosting costs money on their plan, payouts go to the destination you name, and real payments can then arrive. Until the human answers yes, do not deploy, sign in, change a payout destination, or spend. After a yes, continue to [deploying](deploying.md). After a no or no answer, stop at the local result.

# Operate an existing service

Resolve the requested service and organization with `dvmctl list`, `dvmctl info <slug>`, and `dvmctl whoami`. Confirm them from output before a remote change. Read the [dvmctl reference](https://dvmkit.com/docs/cli-dvmctl.md) for exact flags and output; do not load every operation below.

## Inspect health

Use `status` for compute state, `metrics` for the relevant time window, and `events` or `logs` for the incident. Logs can be raw text. Correlate the job and deployment IDs before acting on an error from an older revision.

A running process does not prove the handler or payment path works. Verify an appropriate capability call after a repair. Route an uncertain job, deploy, or payment outcome to [recovery](recovery.md).

## Inspect earnings and collect payouts

For a DVM mounted under a path, pass `--mount-prefix /feed` to its admin commands (`credit`, `refund`, `content-holds`, `melt-pending`, or `rotate`). Use a leading slash and no trailing slash. The prefix is appended to `--endpoint` or the platform-resolved URL; if that URL already includes the full mount path, omit `--mount-prefix`. Identity and refund-capability probes use the same mount. `destroy` also accepts the option for its admin liability lookup.

Use `dvmctl revenue summary` for totals and `revenue events` or `revenue csv` for the requested period and organization. Report these as earnings, not a wallet balance.

For Cashu, confirm the intended Lightning payout destination with the service configuration. Set or change it only within authorization using `dvmctl set-payout`. Run `dvmctl melt-pending <slug>` for a pass or its documented watch mode for continued service, then inspect `dvmctl melt-status` and the destination's receipt evidence.

Keep the refund and payout roles separate. The worker can use `DVMKIT_REFUND_NWC_URL` to buy ecash for caller refunds and `DVMKIT_MELT_PAYOUT_NWC_URL` to receive builder payouts. Supply these through its secret environment. The DVM's `DVMKIT_NWC_RECEIVE_URI` only receives Lightning credit payments. Never reuse a send-capable connection as that receiving credential.

If caller refunds remain or drain state cannot be read, preserve the payout hold and use [recovery](recovery.md). Do not treat an unavailable liability query as a zero balance.

For stablecoins, verify the configured network and recipient, then inspect the transfer or channel settlement evidence. Keep required close observers running. For opted-in one-payment credit refunds, inspect `dvmctl credit drains-owed`, perform only the authorized transfer, and record the real transaction with `credit drain-settle`. Never record a payment merely to clear the queue. For hosted Tempo builder payout reports, inspect `dvmctl credit tempo-close-reports`; follow the [close-report reference](references/tempo-close-reports.md) for retry or write-off.

## Change the service

For an authorized completed-job refund, run `dvmctl refund <job-id> --dvm <slug>` to inspect the local intent, then repeat it with `--confirm`. No HTTP is sent without confirmation. Omit `--amount` for the remaining unrefunded charge, or supply a positive decimal in the job's credit currency. The default refund ID is stable across retries and equivalent decimal spellings. Preserve the original arguments and reason after an interruption. Use a new `--refund-id` only for a deliberate additional partial refund of the same amount. The money returns to the caller's credit for reuse or `dvm credit drain <dvm>`; a replay reports the original refund and balance snapshot, not the current balance.

Completed-job refunds require a persistent store and platform refund reporting on SDK `0.11.0-rc.1` or a compatible later release. Before activation, pause monetary writes and upgrade all processes sharing the credit database and report queue, including funding writers and retry workers. Mixed-version monetary history and rollback after refund state exists need a state compatibility assessment; see the [SDK upgrade details](https://github.com/dvmkit/sdk/blob/v0.11.0-rc.1/CHANGELOG.md). Per-job payments, closed credits, Tempo channel payments, and x402 batch-channel payments cannot be refunded through this command. Missing historical payment or reopening evidence requires operator inspection; retrying or current exchange rates cannot establish it. Follow each refusal's `hint` and preserve recovery evidence.

Choose the command matching the requested change. Use [deploying](deploying.md) for a new revision. Use restart, scale, environment, domain, or database commands only after checking their target and consequences in the reference. A machine restart does not repair a missing payment record.

Before a transfer, inspect the current owner, intended destination organization, and custody consequences. After transfer, verify the resulting owner and any pending treasury re-key. Follow the required redeployment before reporting payouts ready.

For temporary suspension, use the documented pause/resume path and verify availability afterward. For permanent removal or data deletion, read [retirement](retirement.md) first.

Close with the observed state, change made, and remaining action. Report a payout only when transfer evidence supports it; keep earnings, pending settlement, and funds delivered distinct.

## Per-service payout rail preferences

Run `dvmctl payout-routing <slug>` to read the stored Cashu, Tempo, and Base preferences. Add `--org <handle>` to override the saved organization context; the slug is resolved within that organization. Reading and updating require an organization admin or owner.

Supply any subset of `--cashu <true|false|null>`, `--tempo <true|false|null>`, and `--base <true|false|null>` to update only those preferences. For example, `dvmctl payout-routing my-dvm --cashu false --tempo null` declines Cashu and resets Tempo to inherit, leaving Base unchanged. Values must be exactly `true`, `false`, or `null`.

`false` declines a rail; both `true` and `null` inherit the account setting and cannot override an account disable. These are stored preferences applied at the next deploy, not the running machine's payment configuration. Saving does not deploy, edit environment secrets, or change account settings. Output defaults to JSON with all three nullable `accept_*` preferences and `applies_on: "next_deploy"`; add `--human` for an explanation. Use the [deployment procedure](deploying.md) when ready to apply the saved preferences.

## Builder feedback nudges

`dvmctl` may include `feedback_nudge` and `feedback_hint` after a failed command, a first deploy, or a periodic check-in. Under `ask`, describe the proposed feedback and get the builder's agreement before `dvmctl feedback send`. Under `auto`, send your own short, specific note without asking. Under `off`, do not act on a nudge; explicit feedback from the builder can still be sent. Never include credentials, source files, or environment values in feedback.

For held Tempo session refunds, inspect `dvmctl credit tempo-wedged`. After independently returning the entire held amount, including any off-path remainder, attest with `credit tempo-book <handle> <credit-id> <drain-id> --reason "Full refund independently confirmed" --confirm`. Release only when no refund was paid, using `credit tempo-release` with the same ID pair, a reason, and `--confirm`. Neither command sends a payment. Keep the original action, reason, and optional audit evidence for replay; current balance and spendable value can differ. See [Tempo recovery](references/tempo-close-reports.md).

# Recover an uncertain or failed operation

Start from the operation that failed, not from onboarding. Preserve its service, organization, endpoint, job/deployment/funding IDs, time window, caller journal, and receipt. Keep secrets out of the report.

## Determine whether it happened

Read the command's structured error and recovery hint. Distinguish a refusal before submission from a pending operation or lost response. Stop dependent money movement while the result is unknown.

| Operation | First evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Deployment | Existing deployment status, active service revision, and events |
| Job or paid submit | Original caller profile, request ID, job state, messages, and receipt |
| Lightning credit funding | Original fund ID, invoice settlement evidence, and a credit balance read |
| Cashu payout or refund | Melt status, pending drains, retained proofs, and wallet or mint evidence |
| Stablecoin settlement | Correct network's transaction receipt and channel state |

Do not create a new funding, request, or deployment merely because the prior response was lost. Use the original operation's supported resume/reconcile path. A fresh request ID changes the operation; it is not a retry.

For Lightning funding, `dvm credit balance <endpoint>` can prompt recognition of the paid invoice. Keep the receiving wallet reachable. If confirmation is blocked, use the builder's blocked-invoice inspection below; do not pay another invoice to compensate for an unknown one.

## Choose a supported repair

Read only the relevant [dvmctl command contract](https://dvmkit.com/docs/cli-dvmctl.md) before invoking a repair:

- `credit blocked` inspects Lightning invoice problems; `credit reconcile` checks the existing payment evidence.
- `credit x402-wedged` and `credit x402-reconcile` inspect and reconcile x402 settlement.
- `credit tempo-wedged` and `credit tempo-reconcile` inspect and reconcile Tempo drains. A landed close covering the debit can be reconciled. For a short refund, independently return any remainder, then use `credit tempo-book <handle> <credit-id> <drain-id> --reason "Full refund independently confirmed" --confirm` to attest to the whole refund. Use `credit tempo-release <handle> <credit-id> <drain-id> --reason "No refund paid" --confirm` only when no refund was paid. Both accept optional `--evidence` as an audit note/reference, never chain proof, and send no HTTP without `--confirm`. Replay the same action, reason, and evidence after an interruption. Restored balance can remain unspendable. Read the [Tempo reference](references/tempo-close-reports.md) for refusal guidance and evidence semantics. Written-off held rows remain visible but excluded from action counts; `--include-resolved` adds terminal decisions.
- `credit tempo-close-reports`, `credit tempo-close-report-retry`, and `credit tempo-close-report-write-off` manage the builder's payout reports. Read the [Tempo close-report reference](references/tempo-close-reports.md) before acting.
- `credit drains-owed` identifies manual stablecoin refunds. `credit drain-settle` records a transfer that actually happened; it does not send the funds.
- `melt-pending` services ecash refunds before builder payout. Restore missing worker credentials or connectivity without removing the refund hold.

A write-off has an obligation-specific meaning: a Tempo drain write-off only annotates a still-held debit; a channel close-report write-off abandons the builder payout report. Explain the exact obligation and consequence and require authorization for that loss before using a write-off command. Do not substitute write-off for a reconciliation that has not established the outcome.

For runtime failure, inspect current logs, configuration names, dependencies, and persistence before restarting or rolling back. A rollback does not undo external transfers or necessarily restore an earlier database schema. Never rotate or delete recovery keys as a general repair. If a rotation reached the DVM but its platform update is pending, follow the CLI's synchronization hint; rotating again would create another key change.

## Get help from a person

When the tool cannot resolve the problem, or the failure is on the platform or the account, tell the human where to get help: the dvmkit builder Discord at https://discord.gg/aJ8BwVj5G2 first, and `support@dvmkit.com` as the fallback for account access, billing, or a problem that must stay private. When a command's error output has a `help` field, relay that link. Give the human the trace or deploy ID, the service slug, the `dvmctl` version, and what you tried. Never include secrets or recovery words.

## Verify and retain evidence

Re-read the original operation and its liability or balance after the repair. Verify the actual job result or funds movement as relevant. A repair command exiting successfully is not sufficient if the underlying state is still pending.

Retain records until all dependent obligations resolve. If evidence is unavailable, report the precise unknown state and the dependency needed to resolve it. Do not claim zero liability or destroy the service to make an unresolved queue disappear. Permanent shutdown belongs in [retirement](retirement.md).

# Retire a service

Use this only when the user intends to stop offering the service or remove its infrastructure. For an incident or uncertain payment, use [recovery](recovery.md).

## Establish the shutdown scope

Confirm the service, organization, and endpoint from current output. Distinguish a temporary pause from permanent removal, including whether the database should remain. Existing authorization counts, but an instruction to stop compute does not imply permission to delete financial records.

Read the [destroy and pause contracts](https://dvmkit.com/docs/cli-dvmctl.md) before changing availability. Pause stops routing and compute while preserving service resources. It also makes the service unavailable to callers, so it is not a way to keep serving refunds.

## Account for obligations

Inspect active jobs, open caller credit, pending drains, unsettled channels, pending ecash, and payout state. Use the operational and credit inspection commands for the configured methods. Reconcile unavailable or inconsistent evidence before treating anything as empty.

Preserve the database, signing identity, Cashu recovery material, and caller-refund records needed to complete outstanding work. Keep the receiving wallet and settlement/refund workers available for obligations that still depend on them. Lightning payments already received can still back unused caller credit.

Resolve refunds and settlements through their normal paths and verify delivery. Do not send an unrelated manual transfer for a channel-backed refund or record a transfer that has not occurred. Route stuck states to [recovery](recovery.md).

## Remove only the authorized resources

Use the platform's wind-down behavior when destruction reports outstanding credit. Inspect the returned state and continue serving the outstanding obligations; a `winding_down` response is not completed removal.

When permanent destruction is authorized and its consequences are understood, finish and verify [financial export](references/financial-export.md), then invoke `dvmctl destroy "$DVM_HANDLE" --org "$DVM_ORG" --confirm` with the same selected service and organization used for DB access, adding `--keep-db` when retaining the database is part of the shutdown plan. The default can remove the paired database. Never choose the default while that database is still needed for recovery.

For self-hosted services, remove infrastructure through the host's tools only after the same obligation check. Cloud commands do not destroy the separately managed host.

## Confirm the final state

Verify service availability, platform state, remaining infrastructure, and unresolved balances. Preserve necessary financial evidence before revoking the credentials required to inspect it. Revoke obsolete platform and wallet access deliberately; destroying compute does not revoke external connections.

Report what stopped, what was removed, what remains retained or payable, and who must act next. Call retirement complete only when the agreed resources and obligations are accounted for.

Complete and verify the export before either destruction variant removes compute. The builder owns the export file; platform-retained financial history does not replace it. `--keep-db` preserves storage but removes the running machine and database tunnel. Later DB access requires redeploying and reattaching that retained database through the supported deployment flow. Keep the selected `--org` on DB connect/proxy and destruction commands, or deliberately confirm the active organization context before omitting it.

# Test a capability and its payment path

Select the evidence the change needs. Handler tests establish behavior; live provider checks establish an external request contract; a paid call establishes the selected payment path. Do not substitute one for another.

## Before moving value

1. Read the approved price, test rail, and spend cap. A per-call cap does not authorize an arbitrary wallet deposit. Establish any funding amount and provider spend separately if not already approved.
2. Verify the endpoint, advertised capability, network or mint, and payment destination. Read the dev banner. Local execution does not imply fake funds.
3. Isolate the test caller with a fresh `DVM_CONFIG_DIR`. Keep it separate from the builder's recovery material and normal caller wallet. Use the admitted caller CLI version.
4. Run `dvmctl validate`, `dvmctl doctor`, and the project's checks. For a paid upstream API, verify the request shape against the live provider within the authorized spend before selling the capability.

## Select one payment recipe

Load only the recipe needed for the approved test:

| Payment path | Procedure | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cashu per-job | [Cashu test](references/local-cashu-test.md) | Owned or approved hosted FakeWallet mint |
| x402 per-job | [x402 test](references/local-x402-test.md) | Base Sepolia test USDC |
| Tempo per-job | [Tempo test](references/local-tempo-test.md) | Moderato test currency |
| Lightning-funded credit | [Lightning acceptance](references/lightning-credit-test.md) | Durable service and separately approved wallet-backed funds |

The three local per-job recipes use disposable dev state without Postgres. Lightning funds prepaid credit and needs durable storage; do not invent a per-job Lightning test or substitute a production wallet into a fake-money recipe.

Apply the actual approved input and caps to the recipe before running it. Read its prerequisites and cleanup behavior first. Do not automatically increase a cap or change a network to make a refusal disappear.

## Assess the result

Require a terminal job, the expected content, all advertised artifacts, and a verified stored receipt. Verify the rail and amount against the unpaid quote or the selected credit draw. Require independent wallet or chain evidence for the original payment. Receipt verification alone does not establish where value arrived.

A successful test establishes only that endpoint, revision, rail, and network. State those limits in the result. Keep nonsecret evidence needed to reproduce the finding.

On a pending or lost response, keep the caller profile and operation identifiers and continue through [recovery](recovery.md). Cleanup is allowed only after outcomes are known and remaining value is recovered or explicitly disposable. A pending payment journal is recovery material, not a temporary file to delete.
